body:
Control [11.6.2](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x20-V11-Cryptography.md#v116-public-key-cryptography) is also required for applications with moderate security.

The high security requirements can be addressed with a new control, see issue #2986.

comments.body:
I support this being bumped to a level 2.

CC @randomstuff @danielcuthbert 

The current text is:

_11.6.2 Verify that industry-proven cryptographic algorithms are used for key exchange (such as Diffie-Hellman) with a focus on ensuring that key exchange mechanisms use secure parameters. This will prevent attacks on the key establishment process which could lead to adversary-in-the-middle attacks or cryptographic breaks._
I totally agree that it should be L2.
Hey @danielcuthbert @elarlang @tghosth are we ok to go to PR on this one? I'm going to go for it but stop me if it's not appropriate.

See discussion here:
https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2695

The tl;dr is that the TLS aspects of key exchange are handled in a different chapter and therefore the actual applicability of this requirement is very niche. We have somewhere between 150 and 200 requirements in L2 and we need to make tricky but necessary decisions about what gets pushed up to L3 which is what we did here.

> See discussion here: [#2695](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2695)
> 
> The tl;dr is that the TLS aspects of key exchange are handled in a different chapter and therefore the actual applicability of this requirement is very niche. We have somewhere between 150 and 200 requirements in L2 and we need to make tricky but necessary decisions about what gets pushed up to L3 which is what we did here.

Josh, there was very little discussion on this exact issue in the thread you cited. This is as good as any a place to discuss it. It's a very small change, approved by one of the main cryptographic leads. This is a small change that three of us now agree with. Please consider differently.

@jmanico there was a fair amount of back and forth specifically about this requirement (formerly 6.7.1) and I don't think it is fair to dismiss my request that that is referenced. In fact, you even suggested merging this requirement into a larger TLS requirement.

@randomstuff: It feels like [in the previous thread](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2695) you agreed that this was a niche issue outside TLS and you even supported @jmanico's proposal to merge into TLS. Do you have further thoughts on why we should reverse this requirement (which again is separate to TLS considerations) back to L2?

> @jmanico there was a fair amount of back and forth specifically about this requirement (formerly 6.7.1) and I don't think it is fair to dismiss my request that that is referenced. In fact, you even suggested merging this requirement into a larger TLS requirement.

Ah, the number change why I missed it when I searched in the issue tracker. It was not intentional.
But again several folks like level 2 for this one. And I don't think forcing levels based on level counts is the right way to go. It should be based only on risk analysis.

> But again several folks like level 2 for this one. And I don't think forcing levels based on level counts is the right way to go. It should be based only on risk analysis.

I have not yet seen an explanation or risk analysis for this requirement having L2 outside of TLS use cases

> > But again several folks like level 2 for this one. And I don't think forcing levels based on level counts is the right way to go. It should be based only on risk analysis.
> 
> I have not yet seen an explanation or risk analysis for this requirement having L2 outside of TLS use cases

The OP discussed it briefly.

> The OP discussed it briefly.

I didn't see anything on this thread and I have responded to the points in the previous thread
Hey @ingo-rauner @randomstuff I agree with you both, but @tghosth and @elarlang do not. Do you have any other comments of suggestions as to why we want this to be level 2?

> @randomstuff: It feels like https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2695 you agreed that this was a niche issue outside TLS and you even supported @jmanico's proposal to merge into TLS. Do you have further thoughts on why we should reverse this requirement (which again is separate to TLS considerations) back to L2?

AFAIU, after rereading all this is that the motivation/reasoning of making 11.6.2 L3 (and not L2) is that we are expected to have another requirement which requires resistance to MITM attacks *for TLS*. I am not sure we do. Reading V12, we do have 12.3.2 "Verify that TLS clients validate certificates received before communicating with a TLS server.". Roughly, this requirement is supposed to prevent MITM attacks so we might think we are OK.

It is still weird to have 11.6.2 which requires MITM-resistant KEX *for L3 only*. People will probably ask about this same question again (and I will probably ask myself the same question again) if we don't do something about it 😄 . If we want to keep this, maybe we might need to add a note clarifying that we *do* have another requirement which requires MITM-resistance for TLS.

Ok so let me ask some questions:

1) We have [requirement 12.1.2](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x21-V12-Communications.md#v121-general-tls-security-guidance) related to ciphers. Do I understand correctly that if you are using a secure cipher in TLS, that implies secure key exchange with no further thought required?

2) Can you think of another common scenario where a developer will have to handle a situation of manually building an automated key exchange process which seems to be the only case where 11.6.2 would be relevant.

> but instead clarify in a note that this is required for HTTPS/TLS servers as part of another requirement.

Any proposed text for that?
ping @randomstuff do you have a proposal for this note?

Possible note:

> Additional requirements in V12 mandate protection against man-in-the-middle attackers for transport layer protection (such as TLS). For end-to-end protection, we do not require protection against man-in-the-middle attacks by the application server in general.

In this case, we would have 11.6.2 changed into:

> Verify that approved cryptographic algorithms are used for key exchange (such as Diffie-Hellman) with a focus on ensuring that key exchange mechanisms use secure parameters. (L2)

i.e. remove "This will prevent attacks on the key establishment process which could lead to adversary-in-the-middle attacks or cryptographic breaks."

I'm not sure about this one. Does it make sens? @danielcuthbert and @unprovable? and @ingo-rauner?

I don't understand why we need to change the wording for 11.6.2. If I understand the concern, all we would have to add is as follows:

---

## V11.6 Public Key Cryptography

Public Key Cryptography will be used where it is not possible or not desirable to share a secret key between multiple parties.

As part of this, there exists a need for approved key exchange mechanisms, such as Diffie-Hellman and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) to ensure that the cryptosystem remains secure against modern threats. **The "Secure Communication" chapter provides requirements for TLS so the requirements in this section are intended for situations where Public Key Cryptography is being used in use cases other than TLS.**

---

What am I missing from this issue that is not covered by the note above?

Maybe the changes I was proposing in my previous comment are not needed.

There are two aspects of it:

1. The requirement is currently L3. I think it would better be L2.
2. The current wording requires MITM-resistance (for L3). I think it might make sense to avoid having a strong "require" on this part.

To summarize, I'd rather have a weaker requirement which is applicable for L2 than a stronger one that is only applicable for L3.

That being said, just adding the note works.
I am going to PR the note with #3052 and let's move on, thanks.

title: 11.6.2 / v5.0.be-6.7.1 should be reduced to level 2
